extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychology, psychoanalysis, literary theory, and readers interested in the psychology of humor and wit
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic/theoretical criteria for distinguishing wit, comic, and humor and for explaining their psychological origins and conditions of effect (Freud's essay-level treatment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between wit and the comic
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic of speech is not synonymous with wit, and wit must be something quite different from speech comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'With a fork and with effort, his mother pulled him out of the mess' is only comical; Heine’s line about 'Professors, students, Philistines, and cattle' is witty. The page argues one must examine independently of pleasure-disposition to decide whether an utterance is wit or comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wit's twofold perception (double face)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wit 'presents to the hearer a double face, and forces him to two different views.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful witticism yields two simultaneous readings: a surface (often nonsensical) reading and a deeper reading accessible via unconscious associations; this duality is essential to wit and distinguishes it from mere comic phrasing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possessed wit vs made wit
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between 'the wit which one "has"' (a native cleverness) and 'the wit which one "makes"' (constructed witticisms); possession of wit is conditioned by the ability to evoke the comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors like Stettenheim are called witty because they possess the cleverness that evokes comic effects; mechanically producing witticisms does not equal possessed wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of speech techniques: fusions, modifications, substitutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic-speech devices include condensations/fusions of expressions, modifications of familiar phrases, and substitutions that replace banal elements by more pretentious or incongruous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (from Wippchen): 'Turkey’s money is like the hay of the sea' (fusion); 'I am nothing but a leafless pillar which tells of a vanished splendor' (fusion); 'Already in my youth Pegasus was alive in me' (pretentious substitution). These techniques can resemble wit but may lack the twofold sense that makes true wit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for distinguishing wit-like fusions from wit
rubrics_metrics.description: In true wit the fused or modified elements result in a new sense accessible via unconscious linkage; in inferior wit-like fusions the second reading is empty and the fusion 'falls to pieces' on analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the condensation leads to no analyzable new sense and remains merely nonsense on closer inspection, it should not be treated as wit (it may be 'stunted wit' or just comic nonsense).

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of inadequacy/insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: Cases in which essential conditions are not restricted produce comic effects because of absolute insufficiency (e.g., a riddle that fails to meet riddle-conditions becomes irresistibly comic).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example riddle dialogue about a herring: the failure to confine essential conditions (allowing absurd displacements) makes the situation comic rather than merely foolish.

rubrics_metrics.name: Involuntary comic of speech (clumsiness, poverty of thought)
rubrics_metrics.description: Involuntary comic arises from genuine inadequacy: clumsy expressions, poverty of thought, absence of distinctive manner—these inadequacies can be comic when they create a large disparity with our expectation of the genre.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frederika Kempner’s poems are cited: their 'ingenious poverty of thoughts' and 'extraordinary clumsiness' produce comic effect because of disparity between expected poetic quality and actual expression. When disparity is less, we criticize rather than laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic pleasure derives from difference of expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure is produced 'from the difference resulting from a comparison of two expenditures' (a comparison of the effort normally required versus the effort actually expended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This difference must be 'no longer utilizable and ... capable of discharge' to yield comic pleasure. If the perceived surplus is convertible to other uses, comic pleasure is diminished or absent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition a: Favorable disposition (mood for laughing)
rubrics_metrics.description: A general happy disposition or being 'in the mood for laughing' makes everything more readily comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In euphoric states almost everything seems comic because of a comparison with normal (non-euphoric) expenditure; audience mood explains why theatergoers may laugh at things they would not find comic in ordinary life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition b: Expectation/intention to be comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting oneself in the right mood or expecting comic material lowers the threshold for comic pleasure; intentionality to make things comical amplifies small differences into comic effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attending a comic lecture predisposes one to laugh at slight differences; anticipation and memory of having laughed can itself produce laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition c: Unfavorable mental occupation (serious imaginative activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Serious, imaginative, or goal-directed mental activity is unfavorable to the comic because it occupies the psychic energy needed for automatic discharge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Abstract contemplation or focused attention on serious aims blocks the automatic comparison/discharge process; in such states only large unexpected differences can produce comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition d: Necessity of automatic/foreconscious comparison (avoidance of attention)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comparison that produces comic pleasure must remain automatic (foreconscious) and not be the object of focused attention; fixing attention on the comparison eliminates the comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: an examiner who focuses on a student's ignorance is annoyed rather than amused; teacher/preacher occupied with instruction often fail to perceive pupils' comic movements. The comic process must proceed unnoticed, similar to wit's avoidance of conscious scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition e: Disturbance by strong affective release
rubrics_metrics.description: Marked release of affect (strong emotions, pain, anger) disturbs the comic because it excludes discharge into comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comic feeling tends to occur in tolerably indifferent cases; however, in some cases (e.g., bitter laughter amid strong affects) powerful affect and comic discharge can coexist, producing paradoxical laughter—this exception is discussed with examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condition f: Promotion by additional pleasurable contact-effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Other pleasurable additions to a case (a contact-effect akin to fore-pleasure) can promote the development of comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such additions support the isolation required for discharge; this is one further condition among several that explain when a difference of expenditure yields comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infantile/childhood roots of the comic (psychogenesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic is linked to infantile processes: either to remnants of childish pleasure or to comparisons that reveal the infantile in adults; Bergson's suggestion of 'childish elements' is discussed and adapted to Freud's comparison-based theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Children themselves are not inherently comic except when they 'act as grown-ups'; the comic involves remembering or recognizing a child's mode (motion-impulse, lack of inhibition) in the other or oneself. The infantile can underlie several comic forms (movement, imitation, expectation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Three comparative loci for comic (other vs self / within other / within self)
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic difference arises either (a) through comparing the other with oneself (other appears as child), (b) through a comparison within the other (the other puts himself on the level of a child), or (c) through a comparison within oneself (one finds the child in oneself).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each locus corresponds to distinct comic types: (a) comic of movement/character; (b) comic situation, exaggeration, imitation, degradation, unmasking; (c) comic of expectation and gullibility. This schema ties infantile factors to specific comic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor as economized expenditure of affect
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor allows pleasure despite painful affects by suppressing or discontinuing the usual liberation of affect—i.e., humoristic pleasure 'originates through the economized expenditure of affect.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Humor is more self-sufficient than other comic forms; it can be consummated within one person without needing an audience. Examples: gallows humor, quips made by condemned or endangered persons who suppress or reassign affective response to maintain composure and derive pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humor's interpersonal transmission via sympathetic understanding
rubrics_metrics.description: Humor generated in one person can be experienced by another through sympathetic understanding; shared sympathetic comprehension reproduces the same economized-affect pleasure in the observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A humoristic person's attitude can transmit pleasure to a sympathetic listener even though the humorous process is fundamentally intra-psychic.
